projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph Perrotti was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Joseph F. Perrotti. Mr. Perrotti served in the U.S. Army, and his highest rank was Private First Class. Joe served in the European Theatre. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Perrotti's home in Willoughby, Ohio, on January 21st, 2003. Joe was 79 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: In east Cleveland, 1710 Collamer Avenue. And that's where I got drafted from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you when -- on December 7th of '41, when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I was senior at Shaw High School. I graduated in January of '43. The next day I went in the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day, the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can about that.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I think we had just gone to church and came home. There was no television at that time. There was a radio. And we were sitting in the front room and all of a sudden -- I get nervous.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, no. Calm down. This is just a conversation.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: They said the United States, we've been attacked. And then Roosevelt -- and then Roosevelt got on the mic, and he said something about, "This is war," or something. I forget what he said.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Day of Infamy speech.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Yeah, something like that, right. And we -- at camp four days, Columbus. We took a train ride down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when the Japanese attacked there in '41, did some of the -- any of your fellow classmates quit school and try to join the Service?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Might have been -- not too many. If there were, a couple. But it was certainly exciting, you know. We didn't know who was going to attack us, but it happens.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you think it would be the Japanese that would attack?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Well, we were so young, we never thought about anything like that, you know, but it was -- then we got scared, you know. We got Japanese people in Washington, and they're attacking us. And I saw -- I went to Pearl Harbor once, and I was by the U.S.S. Arizona.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Yeah. You could just see the top of it. And these guys -- well, they're still there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, in that year or so after the attack, before you actually joined the Service, do you remember doing anything while you were still in school for the war efforts? Scrap drives or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No. We were so darn young. We were 18 and 19. All we were worried about was going to a football game or a dance or something. We never thought -- we got drafted, but we never thought this was going to happen to us, you know. It was the first time I was ever away from home. I was in bed. I was in the -- at Fort Hays. I went to sleep, and I was crying because I missed home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, can you tell me about your training, then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Well, we were -- we went to Camp Rucker, Alabama, and we had all our machines down there, tanks and everything. And I was learning how to shoot a mortar. I think it was a -- I can't remember the milligra- -- milliliters or something. But the -- what the hell did I say it was?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A mortar?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Mortar, mortar. And you'd put the shell -- the thing in, and it'd shoot it. Maybe went over it, maybe went in front of it. And the third time, you were going to get it in your back pocket. Then we fooled -- I fooled around with the tanks a little bit. But then I was assigned to headquarters company and the reconnaissance, so I had nothing more to do with the tanks except look at them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did your job become then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We were like -- we were in front of the people, in front of them, and made sure that the streets were in the right direction and stuff like that and -- that was part of headquarter's duties, reconnaissance. We used to go out at night and figure out things that we were going to do. At that time, the Germans would put -- put wire across the road about this level. And if you were driving down the street, down the road, it was 20, 30 miles an hour, you never saw the wire. Cut your head right off. Then we put -- we had a piece of metal in front of the -- mounted on the bumper, on the -- not the bumper. Yeah, the bumper. And if you hit a wire, that was just going to snap it off. It saved a few lives. Because once the Germans started retreating, they would put -- when they were retreating, they would put -- where the tanks were going to go through, they put the mines. So you came a day later, two days later, boom. And they did knock out some stuff. And then we were in a mine field in France, and we were probing for mines, and we were on our hands and knees with a bayonet. And if you heard -- if you touched metal or something, you stopped, marked it. There was a man from -- in Europe that he saw the way the Germans had laid this -- the mine field, and he was very helpful. But if you just touched it the wrong way, bingo. We had one kid, Ron Terrier (ph), from California. He was scared no more than all of us were. He ran right through the thing and never hit another mine. He was running. He got a purple heart. He got every little bit. We see him every year at the reunion. But we're getting older.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, let's get back to your training. Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: At Camp Rucker, Alabama. From there -- we were there from January until June. Then they sent us up to Fort Knox, Kentucky, where it was the tanks, all tanks. We went to Fort Knox, Kentucky. And we were training just to be a tank battalion. But then we were one of the chosen few that were going to be in this secret outfit. And we went from -- I think September of '43, we went out to the Camp Bouse, Arizona. We brought -- we were like a trained -- and we would get off maybe a stop. When it stopped, we had -- we were on guard duty. We'd jump into a Jeep or a truck, and you didn't get done with your duty until the next stop. It might have only been 50 miles. But if it was 150 miles, you stayed there, right there. And Camp Bouse, Arizona, if you close your eyes, you passed it. It was a little grocery store and just a minimal amount of people. Then the -- we were trucked into the desert. And there was -- that was our camp. No one was supposed to know where it was at. And the next day, we had our -- we slept on the ground the first night, because there were no tents, no nothing. The engineers marked off where we were going to be at, headquarters, A, B, C, D service company. They built -- they made the trenches. They made the holes for our latrines. And we were allowed one cup -- one helmet full of water a day. You could do whatever you wanted to with it, drink it. We didn't smell very good, though. But from September until we went overseas, we had nothing but dried -- no refrigeration. We had no electricity. And everything was -- everything was dry, milk, powdered milk, everything. No meat, no nothing. Because we had no -- absolutely no refrigeration. And at night, we had little pot-bellied stoves in our tents. These were the big tents that would -- four of us would be in that. And we had little stoves to keep warm, because it got cold in the desert. And every once in a while we would -- the trucks would go back to -- the trucks would go back to Bouse to get coal and stuff. And when we'd give the driver a buck, he'd bring us back a dozen eggs and a loaf of bread. And we had a frying pan. We didn't want to eat what they were eating because that was -- we ate real eggs. Dip it in there. We did pretty good. But we stayed out in the desert. That was July, September. I think we were -- I think we sent overseas in March. But the secret of our -- I might be getting ahead of ourselves. We were -- Patton wanted some certain things done. He wanted to teach us how to have warfare in the desert. And at that time, Rommel, they call him The Fox, The Fox.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Desert Fox?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: He was -- he was a shrewd guy. I mean, he was tough, tough on his men. And he if saw you, you were going to get it with one of those 88s. And all of a sudden -- when we were in Fort Knox, Kentucky, my kid -- my kid brother -- my brother Sam was a military policeman. And every night we would go to Louis- -- close to -- I don't know the town's name anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Is it Louisville? I think so. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We'd go and he'd have a cooler in the back of his car and his buddy was with him. We'd drink beer and go to the -- go to camp. And if -- now, when we went to church -- one morning, I woke up. I looked at the duty roster, and I was shipping out. So a bunch of us were shipped out, and we went to a camp about 30 miles outside of Fort Knox. This was a secret enclosure. It had two mess -- two mess halls, one for the officers and the men that were taking the training for this project we had. We were detailed KP duty. We did -- or guard duty, anything. When you weren't on duty, you could go to the PX, drink beer during the day. They didn't care. Just don't get drunk. But we'd sit there and watch the juke- -- listen to the jukebox. And at night, we would buy a case of beer, sneak into the mess hall. We'd get a nice big frying pan, put some butter in there, and we ate pork chops in butter. Nobody watching us. It was in the darkness, because we were stealing all those pork chops from the mess hall. But we trained. And truthfully, we didn't know what they were doing, the other guys, because they weren't even talking to us. They were separate. Then we were shipped out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why was that training so top secret?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: It was the most secretive thing. It's the best kept secret in the world. We were sworn to secrecy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things were you doing that was so secret?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: This project. Now, what happened is they had this tank. I don't know if it had a gun or not. I don't think it had a gun. They put something in the tank that, at night, when they turned it on, it would illuminate. You'd see -- you'd think they were those big things that advertise for things. You know, those big search lights?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: This was more powerful than that. And we were training to fight at night. They would take -- so many of these tanks would be like this. And in between the tanks, there would be like a cloak of darkness. If you stood in front of the light and -- if you could take a flashlight in the dark. Go in a room. Don't tell your wife where you're going. Go in the room and say, "When I turn this light on, tell me if you can see me." Now, she'd be over there, and you'd would be against the wall. You go like this, turn the light on. She couldn't tell if you were two feet behind it or -- you always were behind it. And they would have the infantry men in there. Now, usually, during the war, you didn't fight at night. You set your -- they used to call it a line up for a murder or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And you'd go to sleep. You'd have guard duties, you know, watching everything, but you never fought. We were going to -- we were going to -- after the fighting during the day, the guy wants to lay down and go to sleep. Well, we were going to take care of him there. But Patton got into the act, and he started going across Europe like it was melted butter. And we -- thank God he was there, because he saved our lives. But ...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that particular tactic was never used then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: It was never used. And then we switched over to a fighting outfit again. But they say they used it one time. And I got it someplace. But it wasn't -- it was scrapped. But we were sworn to secrecy. And even though it was scrapped, we couldn't -- well, that as after. We were in Wales. But when we were in the desert, we couldn't go anywhere. They had guards at -- I think they had four outposts. And there were orders, shoot to kill anybody that tried to get in to see us. And I would -- we that didn't go to the school, we would see something going light. We didn't think anything of it. And then one of the -- one of the generals come out, and he told us everything that was happening, what they were. And you'll see it in some of the literature here. But we used to go to town. We had to take a buddy. You and I would go into town. If you were going to get a girl, I had to be right -- because they had CIC watching us. We had our mail censored in the States, but they didn't stamp it. They didn't stamp it. We had an open letter. We'd put it on the company commander's table, bench, whatever it was. If they read the letter and you said nothing wrong, they'd seal it, send it to home. I had a brother Dominique was stationed at Texarkana, Texas. So he said, "Joe," he says, "Some weekend, we'll get a pass and I'll come and see you." He says, "Tell me where you're at." I used to write back to him. I told him, "Dominique, the weather is beautiful. We're out here getting a nice sun tan." He'd would write back and say, "What the hell's the matter with you? I ask you where you're at, you tell me about something else." Could never tell him. But I met him when we went to England, when we -- we went to -- we went over on the Queen Elizabeth, 20,000 of us. And Joe Louis was there. He went over across with us. And we went through Scotland. We were stationed in Wales, and he came to see me. We met one day, and I think it was Swan -- I can't say the word.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Swansea?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Swansea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And he used to send me all the cigarettes, because I was the one that was supposed to be fighting. And I wasn't -- I wasn't doing that much, you know. I was no hero. But he always sent me cigarettes and candy and stuff because he was concerned about me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you make that crossing?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: In March, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: March of '44?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: March of '44. Now, when we went -- when we went to England -- when we went to England, when we crossed the ocean, we would zigzag every six or seven minutes, because if the submarine had a bead on you, he couldn't catch us. And do you remember that song "Sink the Bismarck," that song because -- because they were knocking -- they were hitting these little ships, but they couldn't get the Elizabeth. Now, when we went across, the Mary would come. Queen Mary would come. They were never together except one time. They got -- I think they were going towards England. And they had little -- little boats. They were going around. And the Queen Mary rammed one of them. Couldn't stop. Those guys -- those guys lost their lives. Because we were both together. And if they would've got either one of us, that's a lot of -- that's a big victory for them. But when they sunk the Bismarck, sort of slowed down. Because they -- we had -- we had guys that were in the Service -- I can't remember the name when we talked -- when we talked to them. They were bringing oil over and different supplies. And if they got hit, we didn't get the supplies. But we stayed in Wales. We were at Wales, and we did more training. We were -- now, that was March before D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And we thought we were going to get it right after D-Day. But I don't know what happened after D-Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you part of the Kiddie Battalion (ph) at that point?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell me about the Kiddie Battalion.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Well, we were all young kids, and we were full of vinegar, and we wanted to fight, you know. But when you went in there and did a little fighting and you saw your buddies dying and hurt ... We were damn lucky. We didn't get -- we lost some cas- -- we had some casualties. But when you fought against a tiger tank, you were the loser. We had a .75 millimeter gun. They had the Screaming Mimi. It was the 88. When that hit our tank, they would go right through it. But when we hit their tank, it's like we were hitting them with a beebee gun, bounced off they had so much armor plating. And they had -- all their equipment was a lot better than ours, but we had -- we had more coming, more coming. And when we were beating Germany, they were starting to retreat, they couldn't even -- Patton started going across Europe, he was full of -- he didn't care who you were. If there was one building standing, he'd point to the -- call them. Get that. Boom. It was going down. He wasn't going to leave nothing up. When he -- when he went towards Berlin, he wanted to go through Berlin, and then he said, "We'll take the Russians too." But the politicians had decided that at the Elbe River -- this side was Zerps (ph) and the other side was called Calbe. Or is it the other way around? Calbe and Zerps? We crossed -- we crossed the river, and we met the Russians, but we were ordered back of the river, because that's where the politician says we would meet the Russians. And that's when they -- Stalin? I don't know. Somebody for Churchill. And Truman, because we had the Truman Bridge over the Elbe River.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in Great Britain before you went over to -- landed in France?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We weren't in Great Bri- -- we were in Wales.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Wales?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: From March, until I think around July. We went to France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in Wales at that time?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh, we used to call that, where we were at, Sheep Shit Hill, because that's the -- they took the sheep away, and we had this -- this hill. And we had to put up our tents. And you had all your clothes with you, and you couldn't wash them. You just -- we used to wash them in five gallons of gasoline. Take your pants off, we'd hang them up, and they would dry, put them back on again. We didn't smell too good. And it was raining and raining, and we had mud slides all over the place. But I got caught with a couple of guys doing something wrong, and we got some duty. So we used to go down -- there was a little slate -- slate, where we would get slate, and we made a nice walk to the mess hall, and then we had little paths that we did for our own. We were full of mud all the time. And it was -- then if we went to town, we had to get -- we were put in a truck, and then the truck would bring us back when we were done. But you couldn't go -- just a certain place. When were in Fort Knox, Kentucky, we used to go to church on Sunday. The truck would bring us right to the door. We had to sit in a certain place. If you went to communion, you come back. Back on the truck. You talked to nobody. Back on the truck and go. Because my brother, he went to somebody in the company. Says, "Where the hell is my brother Joe?" "He shipped out. He was on the duty -- " "I couldn't say goodbye to him or nothing."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was in Fort Knox?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: That was in Fort Knox.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you have much contact with the people, the civilians in Wales?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Once in a while. We'd go to a pub, and we had -- they used to have arf and arf, half beer and half ale. And they had these barrels running down the back of the bar. But it was warm. They had no refrigeration. Even in the -- that late, you drank warm beer. You'd get juiced on warm beer. And then they'd tip us back -- I got so drunk one night. I don't remember nothing. They put me up against the rear -- up against the back of the truck. Flipped the -- I had the dry heaves all the way back to camp. But we didn't have too much -- too much with the people. We didn't -- we knew -- they didn't want us there, and we didn't want to be there anyway, so it was even.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you landed in France in July of '44? Where did you land?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh, God, I really -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it Utah Beach?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I think it was Utah Beach. But we went -- we were close to Saint Low, and they had a bad tank battle there with the tanks, and we ended up holding nothing. Because -- and the tanks, you could see the tanks that had been hit. We didn't see any German tanks because they knocked the hell out of us. But we were -- in France, we were in pup tents. And we -- what the hell -- in the apple orchard. That's what they call it, the apple orchard. And we were there. Now, the tent that I was in, we dug into the ground maybe this much. Because then we could stand up in that little pup tent, and we could even put, like, wood and things so we could sit on it. And at night, some of the officers -- well, there was one officer who used to come and visit us. He'd bring a bottle of booze. They were getting a certain amount they were allotted. And he'd come and sit in our tent, and we'd drink booze until 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, and then he'd go -- he'd go home. And he was -- he was a tough guy, but he was very fair. He -- when we used to be on guard duty at the -- in Arizona, Camp Bouse, you had detail. We were on guard duty. You were on two hours and four off. And you walked around -- we walked around the tents. Somebody was around the tanks, wherever. This one time, Got- -- Lieutenant Gotenour (ph) was under the -- he was officer of the day. When he was officer of the day, you walked around with a rifle ready to -- ready to do something. Because he jumps on the guy in the motor pool, and the guy's name was Rivchun, Sandy Rivchun. He used to have -- had a jewelry store downtown. Gotenour was up on the ta- -- no. I forget how it was now. He -- He -- Rivchun challenged him. He says, "Halt. Who goes there?" He said, "Lieutenant Gotenour, officer of the day." He says, "Step four steps up and stop." He stops. He said, "Put your -- put your identification on the ground." And he says, "Rivchun, you son of a bitch." He says, "You know who I am. I'm Lieutenant Gotenour." He said, "I don't care who you are." And he commented. He said, "That's the way to be on guard duty." Because Rivchun was walking around, and he was on a tank, and he tried to jump him, and Rivchun got away from him, and they put the gun on him. But when we went overseas, he used to come by the boat, and he would bullshit with us. He'd say, "What did you think of me? Did I get you ready for war?" He says, "We thought you were son of a bitch." Because he was tough, he was tough. But he was good, he was good. When the other guys -- when we were on duty with another lieutenant, we'd slip into a te- -- we'd go around, and we'd slip into the tent and get warm, and then we'd go out. But don't get caught, because you were not supposed to do that. But he taught us pretty good. We says, "We thought we were going to dump you in the river or in the ocean when we got there, but you were all right."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not specifically?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Thank God, I never fired a shot, but we -- we were -- if we took a town, we would take all the people and tell the people -- [Interview interrupted by a telephone call.]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you want to get that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'll stop this. Is your wife going to get that? [Brief interruption]

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I was supposed to take some pills.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Go ahead. I guess we were talking about the early combat experiences.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We didn't do too much combat, but we did do a little bit. Because at that -- like I say, Patton was going so fast, we couldn't even keep up with him. We were having a problem. He wasn't getting any gas. So the foreign -- what they call, the Red Ball convoy, they were mostly colored drivers. They would load up a truck, four by four, I don't know, five-gallon cans of gasoline. They were traveling through the -- trying to catch up at night. They had the run of the straight road. You didn't dare not be out there. They'd be barreling down. Maybe they went a hundred miles. They would jump out of the truck, somebody else would jump in, go another hundred or whatever to bring all the supplies. Because that's what ruined The Fox. He wasn't getting his supplies, so he had to stand there. Nothing you can do. But we were lucky that -- and then we would be right after -- after the fighting was over, we went into -- we had to tell people that they had a half hour to get -- or an hour to get out of their house. What can you take in an hour? Couple of sheets, this, this. And we had to do it because this was war. We'd ship them -- they'd get shipped out. And as soon as they left, we would take a gun and open -- we used to tell them, "Lock up your doors if you've got anything." We were looking for money or guns or anything that we could take. We'd break -- because they weren't coming back. Then we -- and the Germans, a lot of houses, they had a little pen. They would keep chickens in that. We used to kill the chickens, and we'd have chicken. We weren't going to the mess hall to eat that crap that they were -- the first guy up got the eggs. So you were hoping that you'd get part of the egg. But we were -- we were very lucky. We were lucky that Patton was doing what he was doing, and we just sort of mopped up after him. But it was -- it was unbelievable how fast we went when we were racing through the -- and there's an articles in one of these -- one book about how fast we went there. And then we were -- I'm going to say we were the first ones closest to Berlin. We were only 80 miles from Berlin when we went across the Elbe River. Then the war ended, and then we went to Czechoslovakia, and we started to break up because we were -- we were going to go home. We went there at -- there was a town in Czechoslovakia. Prague?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Prague or Pilsen?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Pilsen, Pilsen. And we saw Glenn Miller's band there without Glenn Miller. There was a kid in the band. His name was Stan Harris. He was from my school. But I never got to talk to him. We were just -- we went there for a little entertainment, and then we went back to camp. Then they start -- they were shipping us home. We got -- we were at -- down by the Mediterranean Sea down there. I forget what the name of that town was. But we were all waiting to get shipped home. And they promised us we'd get home for Christmas, and we just missed. We were going -- there was a big storm out at sea. And the guy that was in charge of our boat went completely around the Azores waiting for this -- this storm to get out of the way. And we got -- we had midnight mass on the boat. And when we were going to -- went up on deck, we could see the Statue of Liberty. That was at midnight, back around midnight. And we -- that was -- we kissed the ground, because some of our guys didn't make it. I had a good buddy of mine. His name was Vanartwick. And he was in the -- it was the driver and an officer and Vanartwick, George Vanartwick. He went to St. Ignatius. He was on this side of the Jeep. And this guy, this soldier was cleaning his gun, and he accidentally shot my buddy George. He was dead. The bullet went right through him, a .45, from here to you, like a cannon. And when I came home, I saw -- I don't know if they were going to bring him back or if he -- they were going to -- they -- I saw the OBs. And I went out to the house. I met some people at Camp Rucker, Alabama, his mother and father. I think he had a sister. So when I saw his name, I used to look for anybody. I went out to visit and the girl -- the girl said -- I said, I'm George -- "I was in the Service with George." And they wanted to know how he died. In the papers that they sent home, "In the line of duty." They didn't say that another soldier killed him, but in the line of duty. And they were -- they thanked me for going out there. But I don't like to do things like that, because I get -- I get too sentimental. But he was a good kid, George Vanartwick.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you tell them --

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- how he died?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No. I says, "I really don't know." I said -- because we got separated. And I says, "I really don't know how he passed away." And I was glad, because I didn't want them to think anything. But that's why they said "In the line of duty." And you just -- it's sort of hard. Now, some of the guys, they would -- people would go to the graves. But if you stayed at somebody's house and you died, that person would -- would go bring you to the burial place, and they would take care of flowers or things. Then the people would bring -- would send them some money or something to tide them over. They were real good. But we have guys going back. Some guys go back every year or every five years, and they go back to where they were, and they see the progress and stuff. Some of the people are still there that -- when they went over, they were still there. It wasn't that long after. And then we just came back. I went home. We got off at -- I think it was 55th and Euchlid Avenue. The train stopped there. We had a -- I took a cab. And at that time, they had more than one person in the cab. They said, Wait, I got to get -- for the expenses. But I went home. My mother and father were -- I walked in the house. I said, "Home." We were really, really lucky. We talk about it. We go to these reunions every day -- every year. Now, one time -- it's on the other side of the Mississippi, on the far side, so they take care of the people from California, Texas. And the next year, it will be on this side. Now, last year, we went to Atlanta, Georgia. And then there was a little town that we went to. Not Atlanta, because from Atlanta we had to take another town -- another plane to Macon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Sure.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And then from Macon, we were going to take -- they had a shuttle bus, but somebody -- somebody knew I was coming, and they met us at the -- and we took a ride with them all the way back. And we went to this little -- little town. I'm always thinking of Baskin-Robbins.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Warner Robins.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Yeah. How do you remember that name?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I saw it --

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- on one of your things there.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: That's where we had this -- the Air Force -- where the hell is that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were attached to the Third Army; is that right? Patton's Third Army?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I think we were with -- I think it was the Third Army, but I'm thinking it's Second Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Second Division. And what was your battalion?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: 736 Tank Battalion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Were you involved in the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We just got there after. We went there and it was just -- we were on a -- I guess when it was happening, we were in France. They put us up the true train (ph), and brought us right there. We were real close. But, again, we were lucky we weren't there because it was bad. And we would be in the -- we had -- we stayed with some lady. It was two or three of us. And we'd have tea with them or hot chocolate, you know. If we had anything that we could steal from the kitchen, we'd bring it. And we'd be sitting there talking. Of course, you were always with the shades down. You were in the dark. We had light, but you couldn't see out. We'd hear -- we'd hear a noise and everybody stopped talking. We -- it would go, pa-pa-pa-pa-pa-pa-pa-pa. It sounded like a motor boat, but they were buzz bombs. If we heard it stop before here, we were going to get it. Because we didn't know what it was. We didn't know that that bomb was going to Britain. And you just automatically stopped. If they got here, you were safe. But we didn't realize that they were trying to bomb us. They were going to -- going to England. And he had -- well, he had the best sinus -- who made our atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And he was something else. But we had a lot of fun too. It wasn't just all work. We had a lot of fun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's hear about that.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Well, with these reunions, we -- I used to be -- I was a boxer a little. We used to -- anything to get away from doing work, I'd say. We were boxing. And there was Ranterra (ph) and there was another kid named Garcia. He was from Los Angeles. And Garcia was -- he must've had 100 amateur fights. When we fought him or somebody fought him, you could hardly hit him because he was so fast. You'd get him in the corner, you couldn't even land a punch. You'd ward him off had his hands. Then we had -- our reunions would last, like, three or four days. We'd register. We'd get a hat. I'll show you my hat. And then we -- different things, different events. This Sandy Rivchun -- Saturday was our big banquet. But on the day before, he had a -- with the cooks with the hotel, he would put on a luncheon for us. It was only supposed to be -- well, he never did anything small, ham, turkey and shrimp and everything. See, some of these guys, they would get that shrimp. They took enough for ten people, you know. And because -- then the guys in the end wouldn't get anything. So I told Rivchun one time, I says, "I'm going to put the stuff on their plate." Everything was in order, you know. "Meatball?" "Can I have another one?" "No, not until everybody gets one." They thought I was a son of a gun, but ... And we did good. And this was on him, Sandy Rivchun. And we -- last -- I think he's gone two years. Now his wife doesn't come either. She doesn't come to the reunion. She only did it because Sandy was there. She wasn't that type. There's some want to go. Now, my wife, she's -- she doesn't -- she goes with me, but she really doesn't have anything to talk about, you know. We bullcrap back and forth with the guys, you know. But we have some good times. And we -- first thing we do -- but this dinner, unbelievable. He did that all the time. And we'd go -- we would rent a car as soon as we got there, and we went every place. We had breakfast together, lunch, supper. And then we'd go end up in the hospitality room and had a couple of drinks, go to bed. The next day we did something else. We went to -- we were at Santa Fe. We went to a balloon -- balloon fest. And we had to get up at 4:00 in the morning to get to this place. And I went like -- I was -- it was warm where we were. It was like this. We got there, and it was cold, I mean cold, my wife and I. Behind -- behind where we were sitting was the big fields where they had -- they had over 800 balloons. Now, you know what I'm talking about, the balloons?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: They had races and everything else. Behind us would be -- or in front of us would be all kind of stands. We went to this -- to get a cup of hot chocolate, and they had these rolls. The guy would take a fork or something, dip it in the sugar, in the melted sugar or something. It would come out. It would be white frosting, you know. Man, we ate that. And then right next door was a place to buy clothing. And there was all kind of people there. The guy said, "What do you need?" I said, "I want a ja- -- I want something, a sweat shirt or something." "What size do you want?" I says, "Medium. How much?" "$24." "Here, take it." I bought one for my wife. We were so damn cold. But we watched the races, and we'd come back home. But we were watching these races. And they had sticks out in the field with a balloon on it. And if you came down, the announcer would say, "Here comes Coca-Cola." And he comes down as low as he would get. If you touched that balloon, you get what's in it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: A certain prize. If the gondola touched the ground, you were disqualified. And they had all these races. But getting back to Sandy -- I forgot what I was going to say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned boxing during the war?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to talk to Joe Louis on that crossing?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No. He was right in front of me too. And he turned around, and I said, "Joe Louis." And he just turned around and walked away. I had a chance -- Joe Louis. I used to caddy a lot. And the fellow that I was caddying for had a -- was in this tournament at Willowick. It was a golf course, Willowick Golf Course. And I caddied for my guy, and he got beat by this Gene Koonz (ph). And the guy that was running the tournament says, "Perrotti, do you want to caddy for Joe Louis?" I says, "No." I says, "I'm tired. I don't want to caddy for no -- " And I refused to caddy. Not that because I didn't like him, because he was tough. He was a good boxer. They say Muhammad Ali. I don't think anybody could have touched Joe Louis. But he became -- he got -- he became a bum. His whatchamacall- -- his trainers and everything, they fleeced him. There should be a way they can put so much money in the bank and give him so much. Because he didn't have nothing when he died. Just like Jimmy Bivins from Cleveland. Jimmy Bivins was a tough guy. Where did they find him? They found him in the attic someplace eating out of a can. And it's too bad that things like that happen. But we'd go shopping with Rivchun. We'd go to a candy store. And she'd say, "I want four boxes of that, two boxes of those, six boxes of these. And I want them shipped out." My wife and I looked. We'd buy maybe a pound of candy, you know. We weren't sending any home. We were -- They were terrific, though. We went one place to rent a car and the girl says -- Sandy had the itinerary. He said, "I'm sorry. There's none available." He says, "I can't get a car?" He says, "Where's your boss? Who's your boss?" "That man over there." Says, "Come here." He says, "I can't get a car?" And he showed his card. He says, "Do you know so and so and so and so?" He says, "Just a minute." He said to his girl, "Get him a car." He got his way. And we'd go -- we went to some good restaurants. And he wasn't afraid. I'd say, "Sandy, you pay whatever you -- and he did everything with plastic. Me, dummy, I gotta have -- I would carry five or six or seven hundred dollars, which was stupid. Sandy would pay. And on the way, I would say, "Sandy, how much do I owe you?" "$60." And I never questioned him. And I'd give him the money. (End of Side One, Tape One; Begin Side Two, Tape One)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you and Sandy do a lot during the war for fun?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Not really, no. Sandy, he won a car in a crap game, I think. But we didn't too much together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You weren't that close, as far as --

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In different outfits or different --

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: No. We were -- he was in the same company as me, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Different jobs?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Different jobs. But, no, we -- I don't even remember the first time I ever met him. I can't remember that. But we'd get our -- we were going to go to the plane. He would say, "Joe, I'll meet you at the gate at 12:30." 12:30, he was there. We'd get our luggage checked out. He'd walk in. And here comes one of these vehicles, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: "You got room for four?" And the guy'd say, "No, not right now." He says, "I'll go" -- he says, "Can you come back?" Says, "I'll be right back." Come back. We'd get in the thing. We went to the President's room. They call it the President's room. We walk in with a buzzer. "Mr. Rivchun, how are you doing?" Hello, Lynn. How are you?" We'd sit down. "Would you like to sit down." He said everything was on the house. Whenever he did anything, he knew what he was doing. Practically every -- they knew him by name wherever he went. Sandy was a hell of a guy. And when I went to his funeral, you never saw so many cars in your life. I mean, he had -- I couldn't count. And these Jewish ladies, they got rocks on their hands. They look phony they're so damn big. First thing she would do, she would check this bag. At night, she'd get the bag and put on certain things. We were in Scottsdale one time, and I invited my sister Jenny and her husband, my brother Dominique and her husband -- my brother Dominique and his wife. And we had a table at the banquet, and Lynn had some pearls. So my brother-in-law Mike says, "Gee, those are -- " Oh, my sister said it. "Those are some nice pearls you have, Lynn." And my brother-in-law says, "You want some of them, Honey? You want anything?" He says, "You want to spend about $400?" She says, "You won't get these pearls for $400." But my sister bought them, and she -- when she went home, she made a check out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, do any particularly vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Not really. We were -- not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nothing else that you --

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We just had -- we just had a good time when we had a chance to. When we had to do what they wanted to do, we did that too. Because you were a soldier, and you had to listen to the guy upstairs. Anybody -- I was only a PFC, and I'd -- I asked the lieutenant one time, I says, "How come these guys are getting corporal stripes, and I'm a PFC?" He says, "Perrotti, I don't trust you." He says, "You -- You don't look like you would take enough responsibility." I said, "Okay." I didn't care. So I stayed a PFC. I was one of the oldest-ranking PFCs in our outfit. I think I was a PFC for 33 or four, 33 months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along okay with the officers, though?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yeah. They were all pretty good. We used to get into trouble with the First Sergeant. We had a guy, his name was Allen, Sergeant Allen. We were only in the Service a month or so. And one of the persons lost his money, somebody took this guy's -- you know, you take your wallet out and lay it -- throw it on the bed. Well, nobody would -- nobody would say anything about who took the money. He says, "Okay. We're going on a march. Be ready at 7:00." ________ He brought us to some road. It was raining, and the ruts in the road were from the tanks. We were falling. We were falling. Then he gets us out so far. And he says, "We'll stop right here." He gets up on a little hill, like. He says, "Now, if anybody thinks they want to take it out on me, come forward." Shit, we were just in the Army a couple of weeks. He had -- he was First Sergeant. He had a lot of stripes. Nobody said a word. But when he went out in the desert, he did something wrong. I forget what he did. And we had to guard him. And we didn't have -- we had the gun, and we didn't have a stockade or nothing. So we just had to walk a lot in the desert. And he'd say, "You won't shoot me if I take off." I said, "Go ahead and try it." We said, "Go ahead and try it." Because if he -- if you were guarding him and he had six months in jail or something, and you let him get away, you served his sentence. So we said, "Go ahead, just take a walk. We'll see -- we'll get you for target practice."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I noticed a "gizmo" on these. What's "gizmo" come from?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Oh, God. They just called us that, the gizmos. Now, this is -- we get this every month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you don't know how they got the nickname?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Really, I don't. In some of this stuff you might see it, but I don't remember. And we had a donkey, we had a jackass out in the desert.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: And we called him -- oh, sheez, I can't think of his name now. What the hell was his name? I'll think of his name. But we used to feed him beer. He used to stick around the camp all the time. He was a big moocher. Now, the fellow that gives us that letter, his name is Jack Gay. He is fantastic. He does all this work, and it's no pay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Now, did you see -- did you look at this thing?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've seen that. I think I -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We were at Dachau.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did go. Do you have memories of that that you'd like to tell?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: We got to -- we got to Dachau after -- just after the war, and we saw these bodies. They would be skin and bones. And we saw the -- they told them they were going to take a shower, and they would stand in line naked. They'd get a piece of soap. They'd put them in this room, close the door, and there was -- poof, it was -- it was -- what do you say?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sealed?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: Sealed. They would turn the gas on. They would die. Then they would take them and put them on -- they'd bring them to the furnaces. Now, the furnace, that's got a big door. And they would have a -- they had a steel stretcher-like. They put the body on there. Flip them, burn them. They had -- you know what a 50-gallon barrel looks like? They had them all lined up, all bones, all bones in pots. Nobody knew whose bones -- some of the guys took a bone for a souvenir. I didn't want to touch it. But the Jewish people, there's a lot -- a lot of whatchamacallit against the Germans. They -- they had money. Now, there's so much money in Switzerland, it's billions and billions of dollars. And I don't know. Every once in a while, you see somebody from the Jewish people, they want to be compensated for their grandfather or something. And when they go after something, they usually get it, too, because the Jewish people are -- well, Hitler -- Hitler didn't want anything to do with the Jews. He wanted to kill them all. He wanted to kill them all, and he almost succeeded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do any other souvenir collecting at all?

sp.speaker: Joseph Perrotti
sp.p: I had a -- I had a P-38, and it disappeared out of my drawer one day at home. What happened, my son was in the upstairs with two or three boys in our house, and one kid had to go to the john. The john was downstairs. Instead of going to the john, he opened the door. He was in my gun ____ -- never been fired. Never saw it again. But I couldn't -- we couldn't accuse anybody because we didn't know at that time.
